title: ps, top, ss, lsof and curl for diagnosis
description: Use essential Linux commands to inspect processes, sockets, and HTTP behavior.

data.text: Linux provides a rich set of command-line tools for inspecting the state of a system. ps, top, ss, lsof, and curl are five tools you will reach for constantly when diagnosing production issues. Each serves a different purpose, and together they cover most of the questions you need to answer.

These tools are available on almost every Linux server by default. They require no installation, no configuration, and no internet access. That makes them reliable even in minimal container environments or recovery shells.

ps shows a snapshot of running processes. It does not update automatically, which makes it useful for scripts and logging. The aux options show all processes in a user-oriented format with every column you need.

data.code:
ps aux
ps aux | grep node
ps -eo pid,ppid,cmd,%mem,%cpu --sort=-%cpu | head -10

data.text: top and htop: live process view

top shows a live, updating view of processes sorted by CPU usage by default. You can press M to sort by memory, P to sort by CPU, and k to kill a process. htop is an enhanced version with colors, tree view, and mouse support. It is easier to read but may not be installed on minimal systems.

ss inspects network sockets. It replaces the older netstat command and is faster because it reads directly from kernel memory. ss can show listening ports, established connections, socket states, and process ownership.

data.code:
ss -tulnp           # all listening TCP/UDP ports with process names
ss -s               # summary of socket statistics
ss -tnp             # TCP connections with process info

data.title: Why ss replaces netstat
data.text: netstat reads from /proc, which is slower and can miss transient connections. ss reads kernel socket tables directly, making it faster and more accurate. If you still use netstat, consider switching to ss.

curl is a command-line tool for making HTTP requests. When an application is running but returning errors, curl lets you see exactly what the server is sending back. You can inspect headers, timing, redirects, and response bodies without leaving the terminal.

data.code:
curl -v http://localhost:8080/health
curl -w '\nTotal time: %{time_total}s' -o /dev/null -s http://localhost:8080
curl -I http://localhost:8080   # headers only

data.text: The real power comes from combining these tools. If curl shows a slow response, use ss to check the connection state and top to see if the server process is busy. If a port is not listening, use ps to confirm the service is running and ss to confirm it has bound to the port.

items: Use curl first to confirm the symptom from outside
Use ss to inspect sockets and connection states
Use ps or top to see what the process is doing
Use lsof if you need to see open files or deleted-but-open files

data.title: Key Takeaways
items: ps gives a snapshot of running processes
top gives a live view sorted by CPU or memory
ss inspects sockets faster than netstat
curl tests HTTP endpoints from the command line
Combine tools to trace a symptom to its root cause
